edge.rationale: Paired numerical data is the entry learner-state for constructing scatterplots.
Scatterplot construction depends on recognising explanatory and response variables in context.
Plotting paired data is a core scatterplot construction skill.
Axes and scales are central to constructing and reading scatterplots.
Reading points and visual patterns is a core scatterplot interpretation skill.
Identifying clusters and outliers extends basic scatterplot reading.
Identifying the case that links two measurements is a micro-skill for paired-data scatterplots.
Maintaining pair integrity is required when organising or plotting paired data.
Choosing the x-axis variable is a scatterplot construction micro-skill.
Choosing the y-axis variable is a scatterplot construction micro-skill.
Interpreting each scatterplot point as a case is a core reading micro-skill.
Choosing a scale is a scatterplot construction micro-skill.
Recognising overlapping points extends scatterplot reading for repeated or identical paired values.
Direction is one of the core descriptors of association.
Form is a core descriptor of association.
Strength is a core descriptor of association.
Positive association language refines direction-of-association descriptions.
Negative association language refines direction-of-association descriptions.
No-association language is part of direction and pattern description for bivariate displays.
Linear-association detection prepares for correlation and line-of-best-fit reasoning.
Curved-association detection supports choosing appropriate summaries for bivariate patterns.
Distinguishing strong from weak association refines strength descriptions.
Outlier influence is essential when interpreting correlation and fitted relationships.
Correlation coefficient is a central numerical summary in this curriculum view.
Correlation sign interpretation is a micro-skill within correlation reasoning.
Correlation magnitude interpretation is a micro-skill within correlation reasoning.
Checking linear context is required for appropriate use of correlation.
Distinguishing association from causation is a key bivariate interpretation skill.
Lurking variables explain why association is not automatically causation.
Causal evidence requirements refine the interpretation of observed bivariate associations.
A visual line of best fit summarises approximately linear bivariate association.
Drawing a balanced line through the middle is a micro-skill for visual lines of best fit.
A visual residual balance check supports judging a fitted line.
Interpolation is a common use of a fitted bivariate relationship.
Extrapolation is a common risk when using fitted bivariate relationships.
Prediction from a line of best fit applies bivariate association modelling.
Slope units are a micro-skill for interpreting fitted linear models in context.
Intercept interpretation is a micro-skill for fitted linear models in context.
Residuals support evaluating fitted bivariate models.
Residual calculation is a micro-skill for residual reasoning.
Residual sign interpretation is a micro-skill for residual reasoning.
Residual plots extend fitted-model checking within bivariate association reasoning.
Sample context constrains claims made about bivariate relationships.
Sample-to-population claims are the central learner-state for informal inference.
Sampling variability is essential for informal inference.
Cautious confidence language is part of expressing informal inference.
Margin of error is an informal uncertainty tool for inference.
Comparing sample groups is an application of informal inference with variability.
Random samples provide stronger support for population claims in informal inference.
Recognising limits of claims is a core informal-inference skill.
Identifying the population is a micro-skill for sample-to-population claims.
Identifying the sample is a micro-skill for sample-to-population claims.
Distinguishing sample statistic from population parameter supports inference claims.
Generalisation scope is a core skill for population claims from samples.
Representativeness checks are necessary for defensible inference.
Bias threats constrain the strength of informal inferences.
Sample size affects random uncertainty and is a core informal-inference consideration.
Comparing samples makes sampling variability observable.
Interpreting margin of error as a plausible range refines uncertainty reasoning.
Comparing group differences to variability supports informal inference about groups.
Evidence-strength language supports cautious informal conclusions.
Cautious wording is part of communicating population claims from samples.
Stating limitations is part of valid informal inference communication.
Checking random sampling conditions supports inference-from-samples reasoning.
Recognising limitations of nonrandom samples supports defensible inference claims.
Judging whether a claim is supported by sample evidence is a core informal-inference outcome.
